description: Five companies are worth more than the combined GDP of several major European powers. Welcome to the age of **GAFAM**.

hero.hook: Five companies, a handful of undersea cables, and a good part of the digital world.

blocks.text: Google, Apple, Meta (once Facebook), Amazon and Microsoft: five companies grouped under the acronym **GAFAM**, all born in **[[Silicon Valley]]**. In less than thirty years they have changed the way we communicate, shop and get our news, to the point of rivaling the power of some states. Understanding how they came to dominate, and the attempts to rein them in, is the best way into the balance of power in today's digital world.

The most striking feature of GAFAM is their stock market value. In 2024 the five companies were worth more than $10 trillion together, an amount comparable to the combined GDP of Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy. Apple even became the first company to pass a valuation of $3 trillion.

blocks.caption: Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft are worth more than the combined GDP of several major European powers

blocks.text: In 2021, the cash piled up by GAFAM would in theory have been enough to buy every company in the French CAC 40 index and still leave a financial cushion.

That financial power does not stay abstract: GAFAM spend huge sums every year to influence lawmaking in Washington and Brussels, and they have become strategic partners of governments. Amazon's cloud division, for instance, hosts sensitive data for American federal agencies.

sections.title: A financial power larger than whole countries

blocks.text: The dominance of GAFAM rests on one precise mechanism: **[[Network effects and natural monopolies]]**. The more users a service has, the more indispensable it becomes to be part of it, which discourages new rivals and creates near-monopolies where the first to arrive almost always keeps the advantage.

To lock that position in, the digital giants systematically buy up the threats they see coming: Facebook bought Instagram for $1 billion in 2012, when the app had barely a dozen employees, then WhatsApp in 2014 for $22 billion.
Google alone owns about 10% of all the undersea fiber optic cables in the world, which lets it physically control part of the routes of the internet.

Socially, these algorithms are built to compete for one scarce resource, our **[[attention span]]**. They tend to push the most sensational content, sometimes shutting people inside information “bubbles” that confirm their own opinions, and helping false news spread faster.

sections.title: Monopolies that are almost impossible to challenge

blocks.text: Facing giants that even American courts struggle to contain, the European Union has made itself the main digital regulator in the world: its rules often become standards everywhere else, because it is simpler for a multinational to apply the strictest rule globally than to build a different version for every country.

blocks.caption: The European Union imposes rules on the digital giants that often end up applying worldwide

blocks.text: In 2022, Europe adopted the **[[Digital Markets Act]]**, which forces the largest platforms to open up, for example by letting different messaging apps talk to each other. Fines of several billion euros have already been handed to Google and Meta for abusing a dominant position. In 2024, the EU also became the first organization in the world to give artificial intelligence a legal framework.

The final issue is **digital sovereignty**. By controlling the servers, the operating systems of phones and computers, and even part of the undersea cables, GAFAM hold infrastructure our societies cannot do without. For a European country, depending on an American company for its public data raises a real question of independence.
Google handles more than 90,000 search queries every second: in the time it takes to read this paragraph, more than 3 million searches have already run through its servers.

The business model based on collecting personal data, where the user “pays” with information, draws more and more criticism. Yet GAFAM are also the leading investors in the technologies of tomorrow, such as quantum computing.

GAFAM combine financial power greater than the GDP of major European states, which gives them considerable political and technological weight. In response, the European Union has made itself the world's main regulator, with texts such as the Digital Markets Act.

title: GAFAM: power and overreach
